set.summary: A Palestinian popular uprising against Israeli rule in the West Bank and Gaza Strip broke out in December 1987 after a traffic accident in Gaza in which an Israeli vehicle killed four Palestinian workers, and lasted until the Oslo Declaration of September 1993. B'Tselem's fatality tables for 9 December 1987 to 13 September 1993 record 1,162 Palestinians killed by Israelis: in the occupied territories 1,070 by Israeli security forces (237 of them minors) and 54 by Israeli civilians, and inside the Green Line 17 by security forces and 21 by civilians; the Jewish Virtual Library also gives 1,162. For the same period B'Tselem's tables record 160 Israelis killed by Palestinians (100 civilians and 60 security-force personnel, in the territories and inside the Green Line), while the Jewish Virtual Library gives 200. The Jewish Virtual Library also counts about 1,000 Palestinians killed by other Palestinians in 1987-1993, many accused of collaboration.

set.summary: Israel and the PLO signed the Interim Agreement in Washington, dividing the West Bank into Area A, where the Palestinian Council took over internal security and public order; Area B, where it took over public order for Palestinians while Israel kept overriding responsibility for security; and Area C, the rest of the West Bank, which was to be transferred gradually to Palestinian jurisdiction except for permanent-status issues. Israeli forces were to redeploy from the cities of Jenin, Nablus, Tulkarm, Qalqilya, Ramallah and Bethlehem and some 440 villages before the Palestinian elections the agreement provided for. The areas were drawn on the agreement's maps rather than given as shares in its text; after later redeployments Area A covered about 18% of the territory, Area B about 22% and Area C about 60% (Fanack).

add_cite.claim: Agreement text defines Area A and B by map and Area C as the rest of the West Bank, to be gradually transferred
add_cite.quote: a. "Area A" means the populated areas delineated by a red line and shaded in brown on attached map No. 1 ; b. "Area B" means the populated areas delineated by a red line and shaded in yellow on attached map No. 1 , and the built-up area of the hamlets listed in Appendix 6 to Annex I , and c. "Area C" means areas of the West Bank outside Areas A and B, which, except for the issues that will be negotiated in the permanent status negotiations, will be gradually transferred to Palestinian jurisdiction in accordance with this Agreement.

add_cite.claim: Area A: Council assumes internal security and public order

set.summary: After Hezbollah attacks on Israeli forces and rocket fire on northern Israel, the IDF carried out a week-long air and artillery campaign in south Lebanon. Human Rights Watch reports that the Israeli government's stated objective was to create a refugee flow toward Beirut to pressure the Lebanese government to rein in Hezbollah; some 300,000 Lebanese villagers and Palestinian refugees were temporarily displaced. HRW counted some 120 Lebanese civilians killed and close to 500 injured; in Israel two civilians were killed, both in Kiryat Shmona, and 24 injured by Hezbollah rockets, and about half of Kiryat Shmona's residents left the town during the week. A US-brokered understanding took effect on 31 July.

set.summary: President Clinton hosted Barak and Arafat at Camp David for final-status talks from 11 to 24 July 2000 (Jewish Virtual Library dates). The summit ended without a settlement, with borders, Jerusalem including the Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif, and Palestinian refugees' claimed right of return the central disputes. Participants disagree about responsibility: US envoy Dennis Ross and Israeli negotiator Shlomo Ben-Ami largely blamed Arafat, while US negotiator Robert Malley and co-author Hussein Agha attributed tactical errors to the Israelis and Americans as well as the Palestinians, and the Palestinian Authority's account held that Israel had offered only a fragmented state of disconnected cantons.

set.summary: Early in the second intifada Palestinian armed groups in the Gaza Strip began firing home-made Qassam rockets and mortars at Sderot and nearby communities, and in 2008 also at Ashkelon and Netivot; Human Rights Watch dates the Qassam's development to late 2001 and its first attack on Israel to 5 March 2002, while its 2009 report counts rocket fire 'since 2001'. HRW counted 15 civilians inside Israel killed by rockets from 2001 to May 2009 and reported that thousands of people moved away from frequently targeted areas such as Sderot. The rockets also killed Palestinians: two Palestinian workers and a Chinese worker in a Gaza settlement in June 2005, at least two Palestinian civilians by mid-2007 when rockets fell short inside Gaza, and two girls in Gaza from late 2008.

set.summary: Two days after the Netanya bombing Israel launched a major West Bank operation, entering Ramallah on 29 March, Tulkarm and Qalqilya on 1 April, Bethlehem on 2 April and Jenin and Nablus on 3 April. In the battle of Jenin refugee camp at least 52 Palestinians were killed—22 of them civilians according to Human Rights Watch, up to half according to the UN—and 23 Israeli soldiers; most accounts cited by the UN put the Palestinian dead in Nablus at 70–80, about 50 of them civilians. For the reoccupation of Palestinian areas from 1 March to 7 May 2002 the UN Secretary-General's report counted 497 Palestinians killed and 1,447 wounded, more than 17,000 people left homeless or in need of shelter repair and an estimated 1 million under round-the-clock curfews; Israel's Foreign Ministry said the IDF lost 30 soldiers in the operation. Palestinian officials' claims of a massacre of hundreds in Jenin were not borne out by HRW or the UN, though HRW documented unlawful killings and use of human shields. The IDF declared the operation over on 21 April.

set.summary: Israel launched a three-week air and ground offensive against Hamas in the Gaza Strip, which ended on 18 January 2009; throughout it Palestinian armed groups fired rockets and mortar shells at southern Israel. Palestinian deaths are estimated at 1,166 by the IDF (709 combatants, 295 civilians, 162 unclassified) and 1,387 by B'Tselem (773 not taking part in hostilities, including 320 minors); the dispute centres partly on some 248 Hamas police. More than 5,300 Palestinians were wounded and, according to UN figures cited by B'Tselem, 20,000 were left homeless. Thirteen Israelis were killed: three civilians and ten soldiers, four of them by friendly fire; dozens of Israelis were wounded by rockets and more than 100 soldiers were wounded. The UN fact-finding mission led by Richard Goldstone, which Israel refused access, reported in September 2009 strong evidence of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the conflict; its main recommendation, which B'Tselem endorsed, was that both Israel and Hamas investigate suspected violations, while Israel condemned the report as biased.

displacement.note: B'Tselem citing UN: 20,000 left homeless; BBC: some 55,000 in UN schools at the height of fighting; at least 66,000 had not returned home a week after the ceasefire

affected_populations.note: IDF: 1,166 killed (295 civilians); B'Tselem: 1,387 (773 not taking part incl. 320 minors; 248 police); more than 5,300 wounded (B'Tselem; BBC citing Palestinian figures); 20,000 homeless (UN via B'Tselem); 55,000 sheltered in UN schools, 66,000+ not yet home a week after the ceasefire (BBC)
B'Tselem: 3 civilians killed by rockets in southern Israel; rocket and mortar fire wounded 'dozens'
B'Tselem: one security-forces member killed by rockets, 5 soldiers in Gaza and 4 by friendly fire; more than 100 soldiers wounded
